claims.statement: Each colonic crypt hosts 12 to 16 intestinal stem cells, those stem cells divide about once every 24 hours, the colonic epithelium renews on a three-to-five-day timescale with absorptive enterocytes replaced every four to five days, and the crypt base is the stem-cell niche from which cells differentiate as they migrate upward.
claims.scope: Human colonic and intestinal epithelium under normal conditions. The renewal interval is carried forward unchanged from lessons 01 to 07 of this block, which established it from the same two sources; the count of 12 to 16 stem cells per crypt is introduced to the block by this lesson, because no earlier lesson asserted a stem-cell count.
claims.uncertainty: The renewal figure is a bulk population interval and not a claim that every cell is replaced together; cell-type lifetimes vary and self-renewing lineages persist, and the same source notes that some enteroendocrine cells can persist for up to 28 days. The stem-cell count and the division interval come from reviews of the intestinal niche and are approximate.

claims.statement: Mitosis is a type of cell division for somatic cells, whereas meiosis is a specialised style of cell division conserved in eukaryotes and particularly designed for the production of gametes; in mitosis the maternal and paternal homologous chromosomes behave independently upon segregation, while in meiosis homologous chromosomes are paired and some of them are physically connected by chiasmata.
claims.scope: Eukaryotic cell division in general. This is the minimum account of mitosis the meiosis comparison needs, sourced independently by this lesson; PREM-05.08 owns the account of mitosis, the cell cycle and their machinery, and this lesson neither extends nor anticipates it.
claims.uncertainty: The statement is a general framing from a review rather than a measurement. That meiosis is restricted to the germ line follows from its role in gamete production as stated here and is not separately measured by this source.

claims.statement: An ordinary mitotic division separates sister chromatids, the two identical copies produced when a chromosome was replicated, sending one to each daughter cell, so that each daughter receives the same chromosome number the parent cell held.
claims.scope: Mitotic division in eukaryotic somatic cells, stated only to the depth the comparison with meiosis requires. PREM-05.08 owns mitosis.
claims.uncertainty: The sources establish that mitosis separates sister chromatids and that sister kinetochores are bi-oriented; the consequence that the chromosome number is preserved is the arithmetic of that separation rather than a separately measured claim.

claims.statement: The human euploid genome contains 46 chromosomes arranged as 23 pairs, and a balanced chromosome number of this kind is called euploid.
claims.scope: The standard human karyotype. This is a diploid count of a somatic cell and is compatible with PREM-BIO-002's statement that the reference human genome assembly spans 22 autosomes and chromosome X, which describes one haploid assembled sequence rather than a diploid chromosome count.
claims.uncertainty: None material for the teaching use here. Individuals with variant karyotypes exist, which is the subject of the aneuploidy claims in this same lesson.

claims.statement: Meiosis consists of a single phase of DNA replication followed by two cell divisions, with no further round of replication between the two divisions.
claims.scope: Meiosis in eukaryotes generally, as presented in a cell-biology textbook chapter.
claims.uncertainty: None material. The lesson is explicit that this replication is an observed feature taken as given, and that the requirement for two divisions follows from it by counting rather than standing as an independent necessity; why meiosis replicates first is not addressed by this source or by the lesson.

claims.statement: During meiosis each duplicated chromosome pairs with its duplicated homolog to form a structure called a bivalent, which contains four chromatids; the two homologs are similar but not identical in DNA sequence, whereas the two sister chromatids of one homolog are identical copies.
claims.scope: Meiotic prophase in eukaryotes.
claims.uncertainty: How the two homologs locate each other in the nucleus is not established by this source and is explicitly left unexplained by the lesson rather than glossed over.

claims.statement: At anaphase of the first meiotic division the two duplicated homologs, each still consisting of two sister chromatids, separate from each other and move to opposite spindle poles; at anaphase of the second meiotic division the sister chromatids separate, producing cells with a haploid DNA content.
claims.scope: The two meiotic divisions in eukaryotes. This is the central factual claim of the lesson and the basis of the reductional and equational labels, which the lesson attaches to the arithmetic rather than taking as vocabulary from this source; the source does not use those two words.
claims.uncertainty: None material for the normal case. The lesson separately records, from a different source, that human oocytes show patterns in which sister chromatids separate at the first division, so this description is the normal course of events rather than an exhaustive account of what can happen.

claims.statement: Cohesion between sister chromatids is released in two stages: the arms of sister chromatids become unglued at the start of anaphase I when the cohesins holding the arms together are degraded, while the sister chromatids of each duplicated homolog remain attached at the centromere by meiosis-specific cohesins that are degraded only at anaphase of meiotic division II.
claims.scope: Meiotic sister-chromatid cohesion in eukaryotes. The lesson presents cohesion as one substance released in two stages at two locations, which is what this source describes, rather than as two different kinds of connection.
claims.uncertainty: The source names arm and centromeric cohesins without giving the full protein inventory or the protection mechanism, and the lesson does not assert one.

claims.statement: The chiasmata created by crossover events hold the maternal and paternal homologs together until the spindle separates them at anaphase I; in organisms with a reduced frequency of meiotic crossing over some chromosome pairs lack chiasmata, those pairs fail to segregate normally, and many of the resulting gametes contain too many or too few chromosomes.
claims.scope: Meiotic segregation in eukaryotes. The second half of the statement is framed by the source around mutant organisms with reduced crossing-over frequency, and the lesson keeps that framing rather than converting it into a general human claim; the corresponding human figures are carried by separate claims from cytological and review sources.
claims.uncertainty: The consequence for gametes is stated qualitatively by the source as many resulting gametes being affected, without a quantitative rate.

claims.statement: Releasing cohesion along the chromatid arms is what allows a chiasma to stop holding a pair of homologs together, because beyond the point of exchange the swapped arms are held to their neighbours by that arm cohesion.
claims.scope: Offered as this lesson's reading of two statements that sit adjacent in one textbook chapter: that chiasmata hold homologs together until anaphase I, and that arm cohesins are degraded at the start of anaphase I. The causal link between the two is the lesson's inference.
claims.uncertainty: No source consulted by this run states the causal link in these terms. It is a mechanistically standard reading, and the lesson marks it in prose as a reading rather than a quotation, but a reviewer should treat it as unsourced and may require it to be narrowed or removed.

claims.statement: During meiotic pairing the homologs exchange segments of DNA with each other, and where the exchange is reciprocal the two homologs end up physically connected at that point; genetic reassortment is enhanced by this crossing over beyond what the assortment of whole homologs alone provides.
claims.scope: Meiotic recombination in eukaryotes.
claims.uncertainty: The further step the lesson takes from this claim, that a reciprocal exchange leaves each chromatid's own centromere in place so that 2 to the 23 counts patterns of centromere parental origin exactly, is the lesson's reasoning from the reciprocal nature of the exchange and is identified as such in the scene 3 source note. No source states it.

claims.statement: In mitosis the sister kinetochores built on the core centromeres of sister chromatids are oppositely oriented in a back-to-back manner and bi-oriented, whereas in meiosis the orientation is converted to mono-orientation with the sister kinetochores united side by side, and this mono-orientation is essential for establishing the reductional division of meiosis I.
claims.scope: The geometric contrast between mitotic bi-orientation and meiosis I mono-orientation, stated generally in a review comparing the two divisions.
claims.uncertainty: The molecular components the review names as imposing mono-orientation, including Rec8, Moa1 and Meikin with shugoshin recruitment, are established largely in fission yeast. The lesson uses only the geometric contrast and bounds the molecular account in a learner-visible callout; it does not assert that the same protein mechanism operates in human meiosis.

claims.statement: The random distribution of maternal and paternal homologs between the daughter cells at meiotic division I means that from this process alone one individual could in principle produce 2 to the power n genetically different gametes, where n is the haploid number of chromosomes, and in humans that is at least 2 to the 23, about 8.4 million.
claims.scope: Independent assortment of whole homologs in human meiosis. The source's own phrase is at least 2 to the 23, because assortment is one of two mechanisms and crossing over adds further variation.
claims.uncertainty: The figure counts combinations of parental origin and does not account for crossing over. The lesson's further figures derived from it, namely 2 to the 46 for a couple, about 24 switch points per gamete and a 2-to-the-47 upper bound, are the lesson's own arithmetic under stated assumptions and are not supported by this or any other source.

claims.statement: In human meiosis the mean number of MLH1 crossover foci per cell was 49.09 with a standard error of 0.07 in males, across 4660 spermatocytes from 56 testicular biopsies, and 69.25 with a standard error of 0.29 in females, across 2038 oocytes from 63 fetal ovaries; the same study calculated genome-wide genetic lengths of 2455 cM in males and 3463 cM in females from those counts.
claims.scope: Human male and female meiotic cells in one cytological study. The female material is fetal ovarian tissue, so the female counts describe oocytes at a fetal stage rather than oocytes at ovulation.
claims.uncertainty: MLH1 foci are a marker for crossover sites and a focus count can undercount crossovers the marker does not label. The two map lengths are not independent measurements: the study calculated them from the focus counts using a 50 cM per crossover conversion, and its own authors note that linkage studies, which measure map length differently, report longer maps. A second study reports crossover numbers of about 50 and about 70 per nucleus in the two sexes, consistent with these.

claims.statement: The frequency of bivalents lacking an MLH1 crossover focus in human meiotic cells differed significantly between the sexes, at 0.38 per cent in males against 2.60 per cent in females.
claims.scope: Per-bivalent frequencies in the same cytological study, from male testicular biopsies and female fetal ovarian tissue.
claims.uncertainty: These are marker-based frequencies, so a bivalent scored as lacking a focus may have had a crossover the marker missed. The lesson notes explicitly that compounding this per-bivalent figure across 23 bivalents under an independence assumption yields about 45 per cent of oocytes carrying at least one such bivalent, which does not sit comfortably with a review's figure of over 10 per cent; the lesson reports both published figures and declines to resolve the discrepancy or to use its own 45 per cent for anything further.

claims.statement: In the same cytological study the mean number of RAD51 foci per cell, marking early recombination intermediates, was 134.07 with a standard error of 5.47 in males from 44 spermatocytes, and 250.28 with a standard error of 10.21 in females from 39 oocytes.
claims.scope: Early recombination-intermediate marker counts in one study, on small numbers of cells: 44 spermatocytes and 39 oocytes, far fewer than the thousands of cells behind that study's crossover counts.
claims.uncertainty: A second study reports higher figures of about 200 per nucleus in males and about 400 in females, roughly half again as many in each sex. The lesson reports both as a disagreement rather than averaging them, and uses only the direction both agree on, namely a large excess of breaks over crossovers and more of both in the female.

claims.statement: In human female meiosis about 25 per cent of the recombinational interactions designated to become crossovers never become crossovers, giving a crossover maturation efficiency of about 0.75 against about 1.0 in the male; double-strand breaks average about 200 per nucleus in males and about 400 in females; and the coefficient of variation for crossover number per nucleus is 18 per cent in females, 1.8-fold that in males at 10 per cent.
claims.scope: Human male and female meiosis as analysed in one 2017 study combining cytological and genetic data.
claims.uncertainty: Maturation efficiency is inferred from the relationship between designated precursor sites and final crossovers rather than observed directly for individual sites. The break counts disagree with an earlier study's lower figures. The lesson uses the variability and inefficiency findings to account for a pattern that a mean alone cannot explain; that use is the lesson's own argument and is not presented in the source.

claims.statement: During oogenesis the chromosomes undergo an asymmetrical division with half the genome segregated into polar bodies, producing only a single viable gamete, whereas spermatogenesis undergoes symmetrical divisions and produces four viable gametes.
claims.scope: Mammalian oogenesis and spermatogenesis, as contrasted in a review of sexually dimorphic meiotic prophase.
claims.uncertainty: The number of polar bodies is not settled by this claim. A separate source describes two, one from each division, and the lesson reports two on that basis while explicitly recording that other accounts give three; whether the first polar body divides again was not established by this run.

claims.statement: Oocytes are formed from primordial germ cells in the fetal ovary and commit in a one-way journey into meiosis, then arrest at the germinal-vesicle stage and spend the majority of their life having entered meiosis without completing it; the first meiotic division is very asymmetric and produces a mature egg together with a much smaller first polar body that later degenerates, after which the egg re-arrests at metaphase of meiosis II, and fertilisation is the event that triggers completion of meiosis II with the production of a second polar body.
claims.scope: Mammalian oocytes and eggs.
claims.uncertainty: The source does not state a maximum duration for the human prophase arrest; the decades figure used in the lesson comes from the separate review cited for the timing dimorphism. Only two polar bodies are described.

claims.statement: In mammals oogenesis occurs during fetal development in utero, with oocytes eventually arresting and being maintained in late prophase I for decades, whereas spermatogenesis occurs throughout the lifespan of the organism.
claims.scope: Mammalian meiosis, in a review of sexually dimorphic features of meiotic prophase.
claims.uncertainty: Decades is the source's own qualitative term rather than a measured interval for any individual.

claims.statement: During meiosis I in oocytes the spindle assembly checkpoint appears weak and ineffectual at detecting chromosomal alignment abnormalities compared with its activity during mitosis, and across the sexes the checkpoints during spermatogenesis are stringent enough that errors are extremely rare while during oogenesis the response of checkpoints to errors is very poor.
claims.scope: Mammalian oocyte and spermatocyte meiosis, drawn from two reviews.
claims.uncertainty: Both statements are qualitative comparisons offered in review prose rather than quantified detection rates. A permissive checkpoint permits an error rather than causing one, and the lesson states that distinction explicitly instead of treating weak checkpoints as a cause of aneuploidy.

claims.statement: Non-disjunction is the failure of chromosomes to separate normally into the four haploid cells during meiosis, so that some of the resulting haploid cells lack a chromosome while others have more than one copy; Down syndrome in humans is caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21 resulting from non-disjunction during meiotic division I or II.
claims.scope: Definition and one named human example, from a cell-biology textbook chapter. Named here only to define a mechanism and its best-known consequence.
claims.uncertainty: The source attributes the extra chromosome 21 to non-disjunction at division I or II without apportioning between them; the apportionment used by the lesson comes from a separate population study, which also records a post-fertilisation mitotic category that this definitional claim does not cover.

claims.statement: Aneuploidy is an unbalanced change in chromosome number at the cellular or organismal level, in which certain chromosomes no longer come in pairs; trisomy means a diploid genome gained an additional chromosome, written 2N+1, and monosomy means a diploid genome lost one, written 2N-1; whole-chromosome aneuploidy involves entire chromosomes being gained or lost, as distinct from segmental aneuploidy in which pieces of chromosomes are amplified or deleted.
claims.scope: Definitions of chromosome-number terminology, taken from the terminology section of a review.
claims.uncertainty: None material. The lesson uses only the definitions and the chromosome count from this source and none of its claims about tumour biology.

claims.statement: Studies of the origin of trisomies in naturally occurring pregnancies use centromeric heterozygosity or homozygosity in the trisomic individual to infer the meiotic stage at which the error occurred.
claims.scope: The retrospective method used to assign a meiotic stage to a naturally occurring trisomy, as described in a review of human aneuploidy. The markers are centromeric.
claims.uncertainty: The review states the method without listing its failure modes. The lesson explains in prose why a marker distant from the centromere cannot serve, which is the lesson's own derivation from the exchange of segments during crossing over. The lesson also records, from a separate study, that human oocytes show error patterns in which sister chromatids separate at meiosis I; that study does not state whether such patterns are misclassified by this method, and the lesson makes no claim that they are.

claims.statement: Among 170 infants with trisomy 21 ascertained in a population-based study in metropolitan Atlanta between 1989 and 1993, with origin assigned using DNA polymorphisms, the distribution by origin was 86 per cent maternal, of which 75 per cent arose at meiosis I and 25 per cent at meiosis II, 9 per cent paternal split evenly between the two divisions, and 5 per cent mitotic.
claims.scope: One geographically defined cohort of 170 cases ascertained in the early 1990s. These are proportions within that cohort and are not universal constants; a different population, period or ascertainment method would be expected to give somewhat different proportions.
claims.uncertainty: The subgroups are small once the cohort is divided by origin and stage, which the lesson makes the learner compute: roughly 37 maternal meiosis II cases. The stage assignment depends on the centromeric-marker method and inherits that method's assumptions. Nothing in this claim describes or applies to any individual.

claims.statement: A study of 218 human oocytes from donors aged 9 to 43 distinguished three error patterns at meiosis I: meiosis I non-disjunction, the gain or loss of a whole chromosome; precocious separation of sister chromatids, in which the sister chromatids of one homolog separate already at meiosis I; and reverse segregation, in which both homologous chromosomes split their two sister chromatids already at meiosis I.
claims.scope: Human oocytes from two donor cohorts in one study, one of small antral follicles from girls and women before chemotherapy and one of oocytes from women in fertility treatment. Used by the lesson only to establish that patterns exist in which sister chromatids separate at meiosis I, which the lesson's simplified two-case model does not contain.
claims.uncertainty: The study does not state that these patterns are misclassified as meiosis II errors by conventional centromere-marker studies, and this run checked the source specifically for that statement and did not find it, so no such claim is made. The cohorts are not a general population sample.

claims.statement: Trisomic and monosomic embryos account for at least 10 per cent of human pregnancies, and for women nearing the end of their reproductive lifespan the incidence may exceed 50 per cent; approximately 0.3 per cent of newborn infants and approximately 35 per cent of spontaneous abortions are trisomic or monosomic.
claims.scope: Population-level frequencies collected in a review of human aneuploidy. These are aggregate figures across studied populations and describe no individual and no individual's probability of any outcome.
claims.uncertainty: The review presents these as approximate levels drawn from a body of literature with varying ascertainment, and gives the conception-stage figure as a range of at least 10 to 40 per cent. The may-exceed-50-per-cent figure is an upper part of a range for a specific group rather than a central estimate. Nothing here is a screening figure or a risk statement for any person.

claims.statement: In the same population-based study of trisomy 21, comparing women aged 40 and over with women under 25, the odds ratio was 5.2 for errors at maternal meiosis I and 51.4 for errors at maternal meiosis II; the authors concluded that the results support an association between advanced maternal age and errors at both divisions, that the association with meiosis I does not pinpoint the timing of the error, and that the association with meiosis II implies at least one maternal-age-related mechanism acting around the time of conception.
claims.scope: One retrospective, population-based cohort of 170 trisomy 21 cases. The design establishes an association between age band and inferred meiotic stage; it does not observe a meiosis and does not identify a mechanism. The authors' third statement is explicitly an implication they draw, not a measured finding.
claims.uncertainty: The meiosis II odds ratio rests on roughly 37 cases once the cohort is divided by origin and stage, so the point estimate is imprecise however large it is; the lesson makes the learner derive that number rather than presenting the ratio unqualified. Confidence is recorded as medium for that reason. This claim is not a risk figure for any individual and carries no screening or reproductive implication.

claims.statement: The maternal age curve for the incidence of trisomies among naturally occurring pregnancies is J-shaped, with a slight increase at the youngest maternal ages and an exponential increase in the decade preceding menopause; the presence of maternal age effects at both extremes of reproductive life, together with the age curves being variable for individual human chromosomes, points towards multiple mechanisms by which ageing affects chromosome segregation, and the genesis of human aneuploidy is described as a multi-step process caused by errors at several distinct stages of oogenesis and exacerbated by a lack of efficient checkpoints.
claims.scope: The reviewing authors' synthesis of the human aneuploidy literature as of 2012, reported here as their assessment of the state of the question rather than as a mechanism.
claims.uncertainty: This is a review's interpretation of a curve's shape and of between-chromosome variation, and interpretations of that kind are revisable. The lesson uses it to establish that no single mechanism accounts for the whole curve, which is the authors' stated position, and does not convert it into a mechanism of its own.

claims.statement: Aneuploidy in human eggs follows a U-shaped relation with female age; within that relation precocious separation of sister chromatids increased linearly with age while meiosis I non-disjunction decreased with age and reverse segregation increased in the oldest group; the study's authors propose that cohesion weakening acts as a molecular clock limiting reproductive capacity, while stating that a separate and currently unclear mechanism causes the elevated rates of meiosis I non-disjunction in young females; and a review of the same literature concludes that loss of cohesin seems unlikely to be the only force driving the increase in non-disjunction in the decade preceding menopause.
claims.scope: The state of the mechanistic question for the maternal age effect, assembled from one 2019 oocyte study and one 2012 review. The cohesion-weakening account is recorded as those authors' proposal and not as an established causal mechanism.
claims.uncertainty: This is deliberately a claim about an unsettled question. The molecular-clock account is a proposal supported by a correlation between centromeric cohesion loss and one error class in one study of 218 oocytes; the reviewing authors of a separate paper judge cohesin loss insufficient as a sole explanation; and the mechanism for the young-age arm of the curve is stated by the study's own authors to be unclear. No assessment item in this lesson keys cohesion weakening as the cause of the maternal age effect, and the lesson must not be read as endorsing it as settled.

claims.statement: Failure to recombine and suboptimally located crossovers were identified as prominent contributors to human trisomy, and over 10 per cent of all human oocytes contain at least one crossover-less bivalent; in the male almost all chromosomes are joined by at least one crossover, which does not apply to the female.
claims.scope: Human oocytes, as summarised in a review of human aneuploidy drawing on studies from the 1990s onward.
claims.uncertainty: The over-10-per-cent figure is a summary estimate in a review rather than a single measurement, and it does not sit comfortably with what compounding a separate study's per-bivalent figure of 2.60 per cent across 23 bivalents would give. The lesson reports both published figures, records the discrepancy as unresolved, and does not compute either into a further conclusion.

claims.statement: The risk of cancer is correlated with tissues that require a large amount of stem-cell divisions to maintain homeostasis, because of the additional risk of random mutation accumulation.
claims.scope: A correlational statement across tissues, reported in a review of the colonic crypt, used here only to connect the crypt's division load to the subject of lesson 10 of this block.
claims.uncertainty: This is a correlation across tissue types reported in review prose, not a causal claim about any tissue and not a risk statement about any person. The lesson does not develop it; cell death, senescence and cancer are the subject of PREM-05.10.
